title: Job 40 — Interim response, second speech opener, Behemoth, and the start of Leviathan

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֖עַן יְהוָ֥ה אֶת־אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר׃

i18n.en: YHWH answered Job and said:

notes.official: **The first speech closes; the address-formula returns.** The verse marks the structural boundary between YHWH's first speech (Job 38–39) and the brief interim before the second speech (40:6 onward). The same verbal form (*vayya'an YHWH et-Iyov*) opens at 38:1; here it closes the first speech with a brief return-of-address.

paragraphs.text: הֲ֭רֹב עִם־שַׁדַּ֣י יִסּ֑וֹר מוֹכִ֖יחַ אֱל֣וֹהַּ יַעֲנֶֽנָּה׃ (פ)

i18n.en: Shall the contender with Shaddai instruct him? Let the one who would rebuke Eloah answer it.

notes.official: **Two divine-name registers in one verse.** *Shaddai* (שַׁדַּי) — the patriarchal divine name (see `qol-mayim-rabbim` for the etymology). *Eloah* (אֱלוֹהַּ) — the rarer singular form of *Elohim*, appearing 52 times in the Hebrew Bible, **41 of which are in Job**. The book's distinctive divine-name register is Eloah-Shaddai-El (the patriarchal-Aramean cluster) rather than YHWH-Elohim (the Israelite-covenantal cluster). The chapter is in *international Wisdom-literature register*. // The challenge is the chapter's signature reversal: the one who *contends* (*rob*, the same root as *rib* — *lawsuit*) with Shaddai is now invited to *instruct* him. Job is being given the floor — his 35 chapters of complaint are positioned as an implicit lawsuit, and now the case-record is offered to him.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֖עַן אִיּ֥וֹב אֶת־יְהוָ֗ה וַיֹּאמַֽר׃

i18n.en: Job answered YHWH and said:

paragraphs.text: הֵ֣ן קַ֭לֹּתִי מָ֣ה אֲשִׁיבֶ֑ךָּ יָ֝דִ֗י שַׂ֣מְתִּי לְמוֹ־פִֽי׃

i18n.en: Behold, I am of small account — what shall I answer you? My hand I lay on my mouth.

notes.official: **Job's first interim response.** *Qaloti* — *I am of small account* (from *qalal*, *be light, of little weight*). The chapter has been weighing Job in the divine-cosmic register; Job acknowledges he comes out *light*. // *Yadi samti l-mo-pi* — *my hand I lay on my mouth* — the canonical gesture of imposed silence (cf. Judg 18:19, Prov 30:32, Mic 7:16). Job is silencing himself.

paragraphs.text: אַחַ֣ת דִּ֭בַּרְתִּי וְלֹ֣א אֶֽעֱנֶ֑ה וּ֝שְׁתַּ֗יִם וְלֹ֣א אוֹסִֽיף׃ (פ)

i18n.en: Once I have spoken, and I will not answer; twice — and I will not add.

notes.official: **The X-then-Y+1 climactic-number formula.** *Achat dibarti ... u-shtayim v-lo osif* — *once I have spoken ... twice and I will not add*. The chapter uses the standard Hebrew Bible **escalating-number formula** (X-then-X+1): *one then two*, parallel to Prov 6:16 (*six then seven*), Prov 30:15-31 (*three then four*, repeatedly), Amos 1:3 onwards (*three transgressions of X, then four*). The formula compresses *I have spoken many times and will speak no more* into a tight numeric climax. // Job's response is properly humble but not yet complete — chapter 42 will give the final acknowledgment. This is the **interim** response: silence, withdrawal, deference. The full retraction comes later.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּֽעַן־יְהוָ֣ה אֶת־אִ֭יּוֹב מנ סערה [מִ֥ן ׀] [סְעָרָ֗ה] וַיֹּאמַֽר׃

i18n.en: YHWH answered Job from the whirlwind and said:

notes.official: **The second speech opens, identically to the first.** *Min se'arah* — *from the whirlwind* — the same source-formula as 38:1. The chapter pivots from the interim response back to direct divine address. The verbal parallel (38:1 / 40:6) frames the two divine speeches as bracketed by the same storm-vehicle vocabulary. // *Ketiv/qere* note: *min se'arah* (ketiv, without the article) → *min ha-se'arah* (qere, with the article). The qere reading restores the article, matching 38:1's *min ha-se'arah* exactly.

paragraphs.text: אֱזָר־נָ֣א כְגֶ֣בֶר חֲלָצֶ֑יךָ אֶ֝שְׁאָלְךָ֗ וְהוֹדִיעֵֽנִי׃

i18n.en: Gird up your loins like a strong man — I will question you, and you instruct me.

notes.official: **The verse is identical to 38:3.** The chapter is consciously bracketing the two divine speeches with the same opening challenge-formula. The reader is being told: the second speech will follow the same rhetorical pattern as the first — question and answer-required. But where the first speech catalogued the cosmos and creatures Job did not control, the second speech will name *two specific creatures* — Behemoth and Leviathan — that Job cannot subdue. The second speech is **focused**, not catalog-broad.

paragraphs.text: הַ֭אַף תָּפֵ֣ר מִשְׁפָּטִ֑י תַּ֝רְשִׁיעֵ֗נִי לְמַ֣עַן תִּצְדָּֽק׃

i18n.en: Would you actually annul my judgment? Would you condemn me so that you may be justified?

notes.official: **The chapter's structural challenge.** Two interrogative verbs: *tafer mishpati* (annul my judgment) and *tarshi'eni l-ma'an titzdaq* (condemn me so that you may be justified). The chapter is naming **the implicit position of Job's complaint**: in arguing his innocence, Job has functionally placed YHWH in the wrong. The chapter is making the structural-juridical observation explicit.

paragraphs.text: וְאִם־זְר֖וֹעַ כָּאֵ֥ל ׀ לָ֑ךְ וּ֝בְק֗וֹל כָּמֹ֥הוּ תַרְעֵֽם׃

i18n.en: Or do you have an arm like El? With a voice like his can you thunder?

notes.official: ***Zeroa ka-El*** — *an arm like El*. The divine-name *El* (the broader-class, the same root as *Elohim*) is invoked. *Zeroa* — *arm* — is the Hebrew Bible's standard term for *strength, military force, agency* (cf. Ex 6:6 — *YHWH's outstretched arm*). // The chapter is asking: do you have **divine-scale agency**? The matching second clause asks: do you have **divine-scale voice** (the storm-voice that thunders)? Job is being measured against the divine power-class. The implicit answer: no. // The verse sets up the chapter's narrowing focus. The first speech (chs 38–39) catalogued the cosmos. The second speech now narrows to: do you have the **physical power** to humble what needs humbling? That power-test is the entry-condition for the Behemoth-and-Leviathan section that follows.

paragraphs.text: עֲדֵ֥ה נָ֣א גָֽא֣וֹן וָגֹ֑בַהּ וְה֖וֹד וְהָדָ֣ר תִּלְבָּֽשׁ׃

i18n.en: Adorn yourself with majesty and exaltation — be clothed in honor and splendor.

notes.official: **The challenge to take the throne.** Four nouns of divine regalia: *ga'on* (majesty), *gobah* (exaltation, height), *hod* (honor, glory), *hadar* (splendor). The chapter is challenging Job to *put on* — *clothe yourself with* — the divine regalia. The implicit framing: only the one wearing these can do what comes next.

paragraphs.text: הָ֭פֵץ עֶבְר֣וֹת אַפֶּ֑ךָ וּרְאֵ֥ה כָל־גֵּ֝אֶ֗ה וְהַשְׁפִּילֵֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: Scatter the outbursts of your anger — look on everyone proud and humble him.

paragraphs.text: רְאֵ֣ה כָל־גֵּ֭אֶה הַכְנִיעֵ֑הוּ וַהֲדֹ֖ךְ רְשָׁעִ֣ים תַּחְתָּֽם׃

i18n.en: Look on everyone proud and bring him low; tread down the wicked where they stand.

paragraphs.text: טָמְנֵ֣ם בֶּעָפָ֣ר יָ֑חַד פְּ֝נֵיהֶ֗ם חֲבֹ֣שׁ בַּטָּמֽוּן׃

i18n.en: Hide them in the dust together; bind up their faces in the hidden place.

paragraphs.text: וְגַם־אֲנִ֥י אוֹדֶ֑ךָּ כִּֽי־תוֹשִׁ֖עַ לְךָ֣ יְמִינֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: Then I myself would acknowledge you, for your own right hand has saved you.

notes.official: **The conditional concession.** *V-gam ani odekka ki-toshia lekha y'minekha* — *Then I too would acknowledge you, that your own right hand has saved you*. The chapter is staging a conditional: if Job can do the proud-humbling work (vv 11-13) by his own right hand, then YHWH would acknowledge his self-sufficient agency. The chapter is structurally setting up the *physical-impossibility* demonstration that follows. Verses 15-24 (Behemoth) and 25-32 + ch 41 (Leviathan) will name **two specific creatures** Job cannot even *touch* — let alone humble. The chapter's rhetorical move: how could you humble the proud-of-the-cosmos if you cannot even subdue a single named animal?

paragraphs.text: הִנֵּה־נָ֣א בְ֭הֵמוֹת אֲשֶׁר־עָשִׂ֣יתִי עִמָּ֑ךְ חָ֝צִ֗יר כַּבָּקָ֥ר יֹאכֵֽל׃

i18n.en: Look now at Behemoth, which I made along with you — he eats grass like the ox.

notes.official: **Behemoth is introduced.** *Behemoth* (בְּהֵמוֹת) — the chapter's first named creature. The noun is grammatically the plural of *behemah* (beast, large quadruped) — a *plural-of-majesty* / *plural-of-intensification* form, naming a single super-class creature: *the Beast par excellence*. // *Asher asiti immakh* — *which I made along with you*. The phrase locates Behemoth in the same creation-context as the human — they are *fellow-creatures*. The chapter is positioning Behemoth as a real-creaturely entity, not a mythological abstraction. // *Chatzir ka-baqar yokhel* — *he eats grass like the ox*. Behemoth is a **herbivorous mega-creature** — the chapter opens its description by establishing the diet. // **Identification.** Modern scholarship has proposed three main identifications: (1) the **hippopotamus** (the standard scholarly default; the hippo's grass-eating, aquatic habitat, and massive size fit the description well); (2) a **mythological-cosmological beast** (the canonical land-counterpart to Leviathan-as-sea-beast, paralleling the Mesopotamian land/sea cosmic-creature pairs); (3) an **extinct megafauna** identification (some 19th-century readings proposed dinosaurs; this is the same creationist-tradition reading we engaged at Gen 1:21 with *taninim*, and it has the same critique-issues — the Hebrew word is not 'dinosaur' and the chapter does not specify). The translation preserves the Hebrew name *Behemoth* untranslated (matching *Leviathan*, the parallel sea-creature); the commentary surfaces the identification spectrum.

paragraphs.text: הִנֵּה־נָ֣א כֹח֣וֹ בְמָתְנָ֑יו וְ֝אֹנ֗וֹ בִּשְׁרִירֵ֥י בִטְנֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Behold now, his strength is in his loins, his power in the muscles of his belly.

notes.official: **Anatomical strength-locus.** *Kocho be-motnav* — *his strength in his loins*. *Ono bi-sh'rirei bitno* — *his power in the muscles of his belly*. The chapter is naming Behemoth's **core musculature** as the seat of his power. The combined *loins + belly-muscles* register matches large quadruped anatomy (heavy hindquarters + massive abdominal muscles for digestion of plant fiber and for support of mass).

paragraphs.text: יַחְפֹּ֣ץ זְנָב֣וֹ כְמוֹ־אָ֑רֶז גִּידֵ֖י פחדו [פַחֲדָ֣יו] יְשֹׂרָֽגוּ׃

i18n.en: He stiffens his tail like a cedar — the sinews of his thighs are knit together.

notes.official: **The cedar-tail.** ***Yachpotz znavo k'mo-erez*** — *he stiffens his tail like a cedar*. The phrase has been one of the chapter's interpretive flashpoints. // The Hebrew *erez* (cedar) is the Lebanon-cedar — a massive tree (heights up to 40m, trunk diameter up to 3m). The image: Behemoth's *tail* is **stiff and massive like a cedar trunk**. This is the description that makes the **hippopotamus identification** difficult — hippopotami do not have cedar-like tails (their tails are short and small relative to body mass). // The verse is often cited in the dinosaur-identification tradition (a *sauropod tail* matches 'cedar-like'). The lens reads the verse: the Hebrew describes a creature with a **large stiff tail comparable to a tree-trunk**. The hippopotamus identification requires reading *zanav* as a euphemism for a different body-part (some commentators have proposed the male reproductive organ — but this is contested and reads in something the Hebrew does not say). // *Ketiv/qere*: *fachado* (qere) for *fchdv* (ketiv) — *his thighs* (qere) for an unpointed consonantal text. The qere is the standard reading. *Gidei fachadav* — *the sinews of his thighs* — names the **hind-leg connective tissue**, knit together for support of mass.

paragraphs.text: עֲ֭צָמָיו אֲפִיקֵ֣י נְחוּשָׁ֑ה גְּ֝רָמָ֗יו כִּמְטִ֥יל בַּרְזֶֽל׃

i18n.en: His bones are channels of bronze, his limbs like bars of iron.

notes.official: **Bronze bones and iron bars.** *Atzamav afiqei nechushah* — *his bones are channels of bronze*. *Grama kim'til barzel* — *his limbs like bars of iron*. // The metaphor is **metallurgical-mechanical**: Behemoth's skeleton is described in metallurgical-engineering register — bones as bronze pipes/channels (hollow, structural), limbs as iron bars (solid, rigid). The chapter is using the canonical Hebrew Bible metal-vocabulary (bronze = soft-strong; iron = harder-stiffer) to name the creature's structural composition. // The verse is the second of the chapter's hard-to-match-to-real-anatomy descriptions. Hippopotamus bones are not 'channels of bronze' in any natural reading. The chapter is using technical-engineering metaphor for a creature whose composition is being described **as if** it were a piece of metalwork.

paragraphs.text: ה֭וּא רֵאשִׁ֣ית דַּרְכֵי־אֵ֑ל הָ֝עֹשׂוֹ יַגֵּ֥שׁ חַרְבּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: He is the first of the ways of El — the one who made him brings his sword.

notes.official: ***Hu reshit darkhei El*** — *he is the first of the ways of El*. The chapter is naming Behemoth as the **first-among-creation**, the *reshit* (beginning, first-fruit) of the divine *darkhei* (ways, methods, projects). The same noun *reshit* opens Gen 1:1 (*bereshit* — *in beginning*). The chapter is using vocabulary that places Behemoth in the **cosmogonic-first-creature** position. // The same compound *reshit darkhei* appears in Prov 8:22 of personified Wisdom: *YHWH qanani reshit darko* — *YHWH possessed me, the first of his ways*. Both passages use *reshit darkhei El/YHWH* for a creature of singular cosmic-foundational status. // *Ha-osho yaggesh charbo* — *the one who made him brings his sword*. The interpretation is contested: possibly *only his maker (i.e., YHWH) can wield a sword against him*, or *only his maker can approach him with weaponry*. Either way: Behemoth is unsubdueable except by his maker.

paragraphs.text: כִּֽי־ב֭וּל הָרִ֣ים יִשְׂאוּ־ל֑וֹ וְֽכָל־חַיַּ֥ת הַ֝שָּׂדֶ֗ה יְשַֽׂחֲקוּ־שָֽׁם׃

i18n.en: For the mountains bring forth produce for him, and all the wild animals of the field play there.

notes.official: **The mountains feed him.** *Bul harim* — *the produce of the mountains* (*bul* — a hapax-style noun, probably *yield, produce, growth*). The mountains *yield up* their produce to Behemoth. Even the mass-feeding-capacity has cosmic scope: Behemoth requires not local pasture but **mountain-scale productivity**. // *V'khol chayyat ha-sadeh y'sachaqu sham* — *and all the wild animals of the field play there*. The chapter pairs Behemoth's feeding-ground with the play-ground of the rest of the wild animals — the same place. The image: an open landscape where Behemoth grazes while smaller animals play in his vicinity. The combination paints Behemoth as **vast but peaceable** — not predatory toward the surrounding animals.

paragraphs.text: תַּֽחַת־צֶאֱלִ֥ים יִשְׁכָּ֑ב בְּסֵ֖תֶר קָנֶ֣ה וּבִצָּֽה׃

i18n.en: Under the lotus trees he lies, in the covert of reeds and marsh.

notes.official: **Habitat.** *Tza'elim* (צֶאֱלִים) — *lotus trees* — water-edge vegetation. *Qaneh u-bitzah* — *reeds and marsh*. The chapter places Behemoth in **wetland habitat**: lotus-covered, reed-fringed, marshy. The habitat-description is the **strongest argument for the hippopotamus identification** — hippos are semi-aquatic, spending their days submerged in marshes and emerging at night to graze. The wetland-habitat detail is consistent with hippo ecology in the Nile / Levantine marshes the Hebrew Bible's authors would have known about.

paragraphs.text: יְסֻכֻּ֣הוּ צֶאֱלִ֣ים צִֽלֲל֑וֹ יְ֝סֻבּ֗וּהוּ עַרְבֵי־נָֽחַל׃

i18n.en: The lotus trees shade him in their shade; the willows of the brook surround him.

paragraphs.text: הֵ֤ן יַעֲשֹׁ֣ק נָ֭הָר לֹ֣א יַחְפּ֑וֹז יִבְטַ֓ח ׀ כִּֽי־יָגִ֖יחַ יַרְדֵּ֣ן אֶל־פִּֽיהוּ׃

i18n.en: Behold, the river surges — he is not alarmed; he is confident even if the Jordan rushes against his mouth.

notes.official: **Behemoth and the Jordan.** *Ya'ashoq nahar lo yachpoz* — *the river surges, he is not alarmed*. *Yivtach ki yagiach Yarden el-pihu* — *he is confident even if the Jordan rushes against his mouth*. // The chapter names a **specific river** — the **Jordan** — as the test-case. The Jordan flows from north to south through the Levant, with major flow-surges in the spring. The chapter is staging Behemoth as **un-disturbable by the Jordan's largest flow** — he can drink the Jordan if it rushes into his mouth and not be alarmed. // The Jordan reference is geographically-specific. It places Behemoth's habitat in the Israelite-known river-system rather than an abstract cosmic-river — though the figure of speech may be hyperbolic (no actual hippo could swallow the Jordan). The reference at minimum locates the audience: Levantine, with the Jordan as the canonical Israelite reference-river.

paragraphs.text: בְּעֵינָ֥יו יִקָּחֶ֑נּוּ בְּ֝מֽוֹקְשִׁ֗ים יִנְקָב־אָֽף׃

i18n.en: Can one take him by his eyes? Can one pierce his nose with a snare?

notes.official: **Behemoth's capture-impossibility.** The chapter closes the Behemoth section with two rhetorical questions about **subduing Behemoth physically**. Can one capture him through his eyes (i.e., by his attention) or by piercing his nose with a snare? The implicit answer: no. // The chapter is staging Behemoth as **unsubdueable by human hunting-technology**. The eye-and-nose hunting-vocabulary is precise: in ANE hunting-iconography, large animals are subdued by piercing the nose (nose-rings, harness-pierce-points) and by capture through visual-attraction (snare-traps positioned in lines of sight). Neither works on Behemoth. // The Behemoth section closes here. Verse 25 onwards (English 41:1-8) shifts to Leviathan — the parallel sea-creature.

paragraphs.text: תִּמְשֹׁ֣ךְ לִוְיָתָ֣ן בְּחַכָּ֑ה וּ֝בְחֶ֗בֶל תַּשְׁקִ֥יעַ לְשֹׁנֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook? Can you press down his tongue with a cord?

notes.official: **Leviathan enters.** *Livyatan* (לִוְיָתָן) — the chapter's second named creature, paired with Behemoth as **land-creature / sea-creature** cosmic-pair. The name *Livyatan* is from a root *lavah* (twist, coil, wind) — *the twisting one*. The same creature is named at: Ps 74:14 (YHWH breaks the heads of Leviathan), Ps 104:26 (Leviathan plays in the sea), Isa 27:1 (YHWH will punish *Livyatan nachash bariach v-Livyatan nachash aqallaton* — *Leviathan the fleeing serpent and Leviathan the twisting serpent — the tannin in the sea*). // The Isaiah 27:1 verse is the critical cross-reference. It **identifies Leviathan with the tannin** — the same word the WoH translation renders as *dragons* in Gen 1:21 (see `taninim` glossary entry). Leviathan IS the *tannin* of the prophets; Leviathan IS the dragon-class creature. The chapter is now describing the canonical Hebrew Bible **sea-dragon** in extensive detail. // **Ugaritic parallel.** The Ugaritic *Lotan* (ltn) is a seven-headed sea-dragon defeated by Baal in the *Baal Cycle*. The Hebrew *Livyatan* is the same name with the addition of the suffix *-yatan* (possibly an adjectival or intensifier ending). The Hebrew Bible Leviathan is the same creature as the Ugaritic Lotan, demythologized but lexically preserved. // The chapter's first question is fishing-vocabulary: *chakkah* (fishhook), *chevel* (cord). Can Leviathan be caught with **fishing equipment**? The implicit answer: no.

paragraphs.text: הֲתָשִׂ֣ים אַגְמ֣וֹן בְּאַפּ֑וֹ וּ֝בְח֗וֹחַ תִּקּ֥וֹב לֶֽחֱיוֹ׃

i18n.en: Can you put a rope into his nose, or pierce his jaw with a hook?

notes.official: **More capture-equipment.** *Agmon* (rope, reed, hook-line). *Choach* (thorn, hook). The chapter is asking: can you use the **canonical fishing/livestock-control equipment** on Leviathan? Implicit answer: no.

paragraphs.text: הֲיַרְבֶּ֣ה אֵ֭לֶיךָ תַּחֲנוּנִ֑ים אִם־יְדַבֵּ֖ר אֵלֶ֣יךָ רַכּֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: Will he multiply pleas to you? Will he speak soft words to you?

notes.official: **Leviathan as anthropomorphic-speaking creature.** The verse implies Leviathan has the capacity for **speech** — would he plead with you, would he speak soft words? The implicit answer: no, he will not. The chapter is staging Leviathan as a *being-with-agency*, not just a creature-to-be-subdued; the rejection of supplication is part of his nature.

paragraphs.text: הֲיִכְרֹ֣ת בְּרִ֣ית עִמָּ֑ךְ תִּ֝קָּחֶ֗נּוּ לְעֶ֣בֶד עוֹלָֽם׃

i18n.en: Will he cut a covenant with you, that you may take him as a slave forever?

notes.official: ***Hayikhrot brit immakh*** — *will he cut a covenant with you*? The chapter uses the technical covenant-vocabulary (*karat brit* — *cut a covenant*, the canonical Hebrew Bible covenant-establishing verb). // The verse is striking: Leviathan is a creature **with the capacity to enter into covenants**. The implication: Leviathan has the **status** to be a covenant-partner — not a beast, but an *agent*. The chapter has now classed Leviathan as a creature *higher than* the kind that could be reduced to *eved olam* (eternal slave). // The lens reads this with attention: Leviathan is described as having the political-relational capacity of a *party*. The chapter is staging Leviathan in a higher creaturely register than Behemoth (who was named as *first of the ways of El*, also high-status, but not as a covenant-capable agent).

paragraphs.text: הַֽתְשַׂחֶק־בּ֭וֹ כַּצִּפּ֑וֹר וְ֝תִקְשְׁרֶ֗נּוּ לְנַעֲרוֹתֶֽיךָ׃

i18n.en: Can you play with him as with a bird? Can you tie him up for your young girls?

paragraphs.text: יִכְר֣וּ עָ֭לָיו חַבָּרִ֑ים יֶ֝חֱצ֗וּהוּ בֵּ֣ין כְּֽנַעֲנִֽים׃

i18n.en: Will guilds bargain over him? Will they divide him among the Canaanite merchants?

notes.official: **The market-trade question.** *Chabbarim* — *companions, members of a guild* (here probably *fishing-guilds* or *merchant-associations*). *Kena'anim* — *Canaanites*, but in the chapter's economic register, the **Canaanite merchants** — the Phoenician trading network. // The chapter is asking: can Leviathan be **commodified** — divided up, sold, distributed through the trade-network? The implicit answer: no, no market would handle Leviathan-as-merchandise. The chapter is staging Leviathan as **outside the economic system** that handles other large creatures.

paragraphs.text: הַֽתְמַלֵּ֣א בְשֻׂכּ֣וֹת עוֹר֑וֹ וּבְצִלְצַ֖ל דָּגִ֣ים רֹאשֽׁוֹ׃

i18n.en: Can you fill his hide with barbs, or his head with fish-spears?

notes.official: **Harpoon-and-spear vocabulary.** *Sukkot* (barbed implements). *Tziltzal dagim* — *fish-spears, fishing-tridents*. The chapter is now asking: can you use the **largest available marine hunting-equipment** on Leviathan? Implicit answer: no.

paragraphs.text: שִׂים־עָלָ֥יו כַּפֶּ֑ךָ זְכֹ֥ר מִ֝לְחָמָ֗ה אַל־תּוֹסַֽף׃

i18n.en: Lay your hand on him — remember the battle, do not repeat it.

notes.official: **The chapter's closing warning.** *Sim alav kapekha z'khor milchamah al-tosaf* — *lay your hand on him; remember the battle, do not repeat it*. The chapter is staging the warning as **post-attempt advice**: if you have ever tried to lay hands on Leviathan, you remember the fight — and you will not try again. // The chapter ends here (Hebrew Job 40 chapter division); Hebrew Job 41 will continue with the full Leviathan description (his shield-scales, his sneezes-of-light, the fire from his mouth, his impenetrable defenses).
